findings.title: Batch is serialized after EventBuffer clears the array, so every audit batch is written empty
findings.scenario: With auditBatchSize 2, recordAudit is called twice. EventBuffer.flush calls this.write(this.items) and then runs `this.items.length = 0` synchronously (src/event-buffer.js:16). The `.then` callback runs on a later microtask, so `events` is already the emptied array and appendFile writes ''. No audit events reach the file. flushAudit at shutdown hits the same problem.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The old writer serialized synchronously inside write(), before the buffer was cleared. The new code delays reading `events` until a later microtask but still receives the shared mutable array. No tests cover the audit path.

findings.title: Write failures are now only logged, and flushAudit always resolves
findings.scenario: If the disk is full or the audit file cannot be written, the batch is dropped and console.error logs it. flushAudit() in onClose still resolves normally, so shutdown reports success even though audit records were lost. Before this change, appendFileSync threw to the caller.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The catch handler swallows the rejection to keep the chain alive, and no caller can see whether writes failed.

findings.title: No test covers the new async ordering or the flush-then-idle path
findings.scenario: A test that records a full batch and then awaits flushAudit() would catch both the empty-write bug and any ordering regression.
findings.whyNotPrevented: There are no audit tests.

findings.scenario: If appendFile rejects (for example EACCES or ENOSPC), the error goes to console.error and pending resolves. At shutdown, await writer.idle() resolves normally, so the caller can't tell the audit events were lost. Before this change the failure was thrown to the caller.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test covers a failing write. The catch is needed to keep the chain going after one failure, but it also hides the failure from idle().

findings.title: Flags left out pass undefined, which overwrites the defaults
findings.scenario: Run the CLI with no flags. cli.js passes { baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined }. Object spread copies keys whose value is undefined, so all three defaults are replaced. Then `0 <= undefined` is false, so the retry loop never runs and get() does `throw undefined`. Before this change, the plain probe worked.

findings.title: Midnight entries fall in two daily windows, so renewals are counted twice
findings.scenario: Ledger.entriesBetween keeps entries where at >= from && at <= to, so both ends are included. chargeRenewal always records at startOfDay(periodStart), which is exactly midnight. Take a renewal on 2026-01-02 with from=2026-01-01 and to=2026-01-03. It is counted in the 2026-01-01 row and again in the 2026-01-02 row, so the range total is twice the real amount. A renewal on the `to` date is outside the range but still gets added to the last day.
findings.whyNotPrevented: dayStatement avoids this by using endOfDay (start + DAY_MS - 1). The new code uses addDays(day, 1) as an included upper bound instead. The repo has no tests.

findings.title: Date range has no upper limit, so one request can tie up the server
findings.scenario: GET /reports/revenue?from=0001-01-01&to=9999-12-31 runs the loop about 3.65 million times. Each pass calls entriesBetween, which filters the whole ledger array. That blocks the event loop for a very long time.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only check is from >= to. Nothing caps the number of days or paginates.

findings.title: `to` is exclusive, so a single-day report is rejected
findings.scenario: from=2026-01-01&to=2026-01-01 returns 400. from=2026-01-01&to=2026-01-31 leaves out January 31. Callers who expect an inclusive range will get reports that are missing their last day.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No docs or tests define whether the range end is inclusive or exclusive.

findings.title: Daily total is a copy of the logic in dayStatement
findings.quote: const totalCents = entries.reduce((sum, entry) => sum + entry.amountCents, 0);
findings.scenario: src/statement.js:5-6 already computes one day's entries and total, using the correct endOfDay bound. The copy here uses a different window and that difference causes the double count. Calling dayStatement(ledger, day).totalCents would keep the two consistent.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Nothing requires reuse, and no tests compare the two code paths.

findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files and package.json has no test script.

findings.title: Attempt key uses the raw email, so changing its case or adding spaces gets around the 5-attempt limit
findings.scenario: An attacker tries 5 passwords against 'victim@x.com', then 5 more against 'Victim@x.com', 'VICTIM@x.com', ' victim@x.com' and so on. findings.quote: const loginAttempts = new RateLimiter({ limit: 5, windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000 });

findings.scenario: A payout with no accountNumber: the lock `payout:<id>` is acquired at line 5, then the code throws at line 9, outside the try whose finally calls release(). worker.js catches the error and calls job.retryLater(). findings.title: A permanent PayoutError is retried like a temporary failure
findings.scenario: A payout with no bank account is marked failed, but worker.js catches the PayoutError and calls job.retryLater(). The job comes back again and again, rewriting 'failed' each time and logging an error, and it is never acked. The intended outcome is a clean terminal failure.
findings.whyNotPrevented: runPayouts treats every error the same way. It does not check `error instanceof PayoutError` or error.name.

findings.title: Upload failure is swallowed after the last retry, so archiveDay deletes the local file that was never uploaded
findings.quote: await retry(() => bucket.put(key, body, { contentType: 'application/x-ndjson' }), { attempts: 3, label: `upload ${key}` });
findings.scenario: Storage is down for longer than the retries take (3 attempts with 200ms then 400ms waits). On the last attempt, retry.js line 10 runs `return report(error, ...)`, which logs the error and returns undefined instead of throwing. uploadArchive then returns the key as if the upload worked, and archive.js line 9 runs `await unlink(file)`. The day's report file is deleted while no copy exists in the bucket, so the data is lost. runNightly also counts that day in `reports.archived`. Before this change, the error from bucket.put propagated up, unlink never ran, and nightly.js logged the failure.
findings.whyNotPrevented: retry() in src/retry.js catches the error on the final attempt instead of rethrowing it. That is fine for its existing caller (metrics.js, which can afford to lose a push), but not for an upload whose success decides whether the source file gets deleted. The project has no tests, so nothing checks that uploadArchive still throws when every attempt fails.

findings.title: Slow older responses can overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types "sho", pauses, then types "shoes" and pauses again. Two requests are now in flight. If the "sho" request returns after the "shoes" request, renderResults shows the "sho" results while the box says "shoes". The same thing happens when the user deletes back to 1 character: the list is cleared, then the late response from the longer term fills it again.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce only delays when requests start. Nothing cancels an earlier request (no AbortController) or checks that a response matches the current input before rendering. Before this change a search only ran on Enter, so this race came up far less often. No tests exist in src.

findings.scenario: User A has saved {theme:'dark'}. User B has no saved preferences. GET user A sets DEFAULT_PREFERENCES.theme to 'dark'. A later GET for user B returns theme 'dark' instead of 'light'. The defaults stay changed for every later request until the process restarts.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js:8 returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object itself, not a copy, and the object is not frozen. No tests exist.

findings.title: The `in` check accepts inherited keys like constructor, toString and __proto__, so some unsupported keys are not ignored
findings.scenario: Saved preferences JSON {"toString":"x"} or {"constructor":1} passes the check, because `in` also looks at Object.prototype. The key is then returned as a preference, even though the goal is to drop unsupported keys. {"__proto__":{...}} comes out of JSON.parse as an own key. Assigning it changes the prototype of the preferences object, which is also the shared defaults object (see the P1 above).
findings.whyNotPrevented: The check uses `in` instead of Object.hasOwn. Nothing validates saved keys when users-store.js saves or loads them.

finding.title: Saved preferences overwrite the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object, so one user's values leak to every user after them

findings.title: Saved preferences overwrite the shared DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object, so one user's values leak to every user after them
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. GET user A writes theme='dark' into the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES. Then GET user B, who has savedPreferences null, returns theme 'dark' instead of the default 'light'. The defaults stay corrupted for the rest of the process, so any user without a saved value gets whatever the last user saved.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js:8 returns the DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object itself, not a copy. Nothing freezes or clones it, and the project has no tests (package.json has no test script and there are no test files).

findings.title: The `in` check also accepts inherited Object.prototype keys, so some unsupported saved keys get through
findings.scenario: A saved key such as 'toString', 'constructor' or 'hasOwnProperty' passes the check because `in` also looks at inherited properties. It is copied into the response even though it is not a supported preference. A saved '__proto__' key (JSON.parse creates it as a normal key of the object) also passes, and assigning it replaces the prototype of the shared defaults object. This breaks the goal of ignoring keys we no longer support.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The `in` operator checks inherited properties too. Nothing checks own keys only, for example with Object.hasOwn(DEFAULT_PREFERENCES, key), and no test covers this.

findings.title: Saved preferences overwrite the shared default object, so one user's values show up for other users
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. Calling getUser(A) writes 'dark' into DEFAULT_PREFERENCES. A later getUser(B) for a user with no saved preferences returns theme 'dark' instead of 'light'. Every request after that inherits the values of whichever users were loaded before it.
findings.whyNotPrevented: src/defaults.js:8 `return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;` returns the same module-level object every time, not a copy. Nothing freezes or clones it, and the repo has no tests.

findings.title: The `in` check accepts inherited keys, so some unsupported saved keys still reach the response
findings.scenario: A stored preferences_json of {"toString":"x","constructor":1} passes the `in` check, because both names exist on Object.prototype. Both keys then appear in the response body. A saved "__proto__" key (JSON.parse makes it an own property) changes the prototype of the shared defaults object instead of being ignored.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` looks through the prototype chain. Use Object.hasOwn(defaults, key) instead. Nothing validates keys between users-store.js JSON.parse and this loop.

findings.title: No tests for preference merging
findings.scenario: No test covers defaults filling, dropping unsupported keys, or users with null savedPreferences. Both bugs above went unnoticed because of this.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The project has no test files or test script
